newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-MARSEILLE TURN TO OLD FAVOURITE COURBIS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MARSEILLE TURN TO OLD FAVOURITE COURBIS.

text.p: Marseille are looking to a fast-talking local to sweep away past troubles and take them back to the big-time.
"On a professional level, you can't really talk about a return to one's origins," said Rolland Courbis, whose career has taken 25 years to come full circle.
"The last time I was at Marseille was in 1972 as a player," the 44-year-old coach said in an interview.
Courbis, who also played for local rivals Monaco, brings with him bags of experience and success, including rebuilding an attractive Bordeaux side last season.
The man from the northern part of Marseille, who started out coaching at nearby Toulon, was a popular choice within the club, not least with president Robert Louis-Dreyfus.
"At least you can talk to him," Louis-Dreyfus said in a dig at the taciturn Gerard Gili, whose side finished mid-table last season without winning an away match.
Courbis faces his first away test at Montpellier, first club of his equally widely travelled captain Laurent Blanc, in the French first division on Saturday.

He does so, however, on the sound footing of two victories in the opening two games at the Velodrome, scene of Marseille's glory years in the early 1990s when they became the first French club to win the European Cup.

Courbis, a confident talker with a sharp tongue whose coaching career has taken him to Bordeaux (twice), Toulouse and amateur club Endoume, has a good answer to criticism levelled at him, particularly from colleagues.
"I'm not going to act like a certain coach from Burgundy who never ceases to state that his team are looking to ensure survival in the top flight," he said.
The dig was at Guy Roux who said as much while guiding Auxerre to the European Cup quarter-finals last season.
"The false modesty of some of my colleagues annoys me."
"Here, that kind of message doesn't wash. So, we show our colours clearly: OM (Olympique Marseille) are aiming for Europe," Courbis said.
He does, however, like to be realistic about the true strengths of his side.
"I enjoyed the humour of Jean Tigana who makes OM the title favourites," Courbis said of his counterpart at champions Monaco.
"Let's be serious, we're not boxing in the same category. It would really need a major faux pas from Monaco and PSG (Paris St Germain) for them not to fight for the title between them."
Courbis believes Marseille should aim at somewhere between third and fifth in the standings.
He said a crucial factor in Marseille's recruiting was to reduce the number of foreigners and go for players of tested experience and character.
"I could see myself struggling with four or five interpreters at meetings," Courbis said.
"I attach a lot of importance to the personality of a player... there's no doubt it's a bit harder to succeed at OM," he said.
"So I opted for players who are regular in their performance and generous in their effort."
Paramount among these is Blanc, who joined from Barcelona after a season in which he was unable to secure a consistent place in the first team with the Spanish giants.
"With his experience and talent, he's going to steady the team. His association with (Germany goalkeeper Andreas) Koepke makes them one of the best pairings in Europe," Courbis said.
"Blanc is a tower in defence but he is also our first counter attacker."

Courbis had another sharp reply to criticism that his team's success in their opening two games was down to Blanc alone, the defender having scored with a penalty and free kick against Le Havre and also forced the winner against Nantes.
"I used to hear people around me say a great team breaks the deadlock in a match with a free kick or penalty. Now I get the impression I'm being reproached for the same thing and I don't get it.
"When we score with a penalty it's because we were in the opposing penalty area, right?"

Courbis understands the ardent Marseille fans' hunger for the glory they became accustomed to not so long ago before their fall from grace under former owner Bernard Tapie. But he expects himself and his team to handle the pressure.

Bankrupt tycoon and former cabinet minister Tapie was released from prison on parole last month after serving almost six months for rigging a 1993 soccer match. He is appealing against another sentence for embezzling club funds.
"The supporters retain the hunger of last season which was a period of transition," said Courbis.
"They expect a lot from us. The bad years are over but some frustration can always resurface. It's up to us to adapt."
